This site started as a single `index.md` file rendered by GitHub Pages with the Jekyll Minimal theme — fine for a static CV, but with no room to grow. I wanted a place to host my CV *and* write occasional posts about research, tools, and methods I find useful. This post documents the migration to [Quarto](https://quarto.org).

## Why Quarto?

Quarto is an open-source scientific publishing system built on Pandoc. It is especially well-suited for researchers because it:

- Renders Markdown, R Markdown, and Jupyter notebooks
- Has first-class support for citations, cross-references, and equations
- Generates a full static website with navigation, search, and blog listings out of the box
- Integrates natively with GitHub Actions for continuous deployment

For a biomedical research CV that might one day host data analyses or methods notes, Quarto is a natural fit.

## Repository Structure

The final layout is straightforward:

```
CV/
├── _quarto.yml                        # project & site configuration
├── index.qmd                          # CV (front page)
├── .nojekyll                          # tells GitHub Pages to skip Jekyll
├── blog/
│   ├── index.qmd                      # blog listing page
│   └── posts/
│       └── 2026-02-19-building-this-website/
│           └── index.qmd             # this post
└── .github/
    └── workflows/
        └── deploy.yml                 # GitHub Actions workflow
```

## The Project Configuration

`_quarto.yml` is the single file that controls everything about the site:

```yaml
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: _site

website:
  title: "Ruisheng Xu"
  site-url: https://Ruisheng5039.github.io/CV
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: CV
      - href: blog/index.qmd
        text: Blog
    right:
      - icon: github
        href: https://github.com/Ruisheng5039

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 2
```

The `site-url` is important: it lets Quarto generate correct absolute links when the site lives at a subpath (`/CV`) rather than at the root domain.

## The CV Page

The original `index.md` was converted to `index.qmd` — the only real change is the YAML front matter block at the top:

```yaml
---
title: "Ruisheng Xu"
subtitle: "Ph.D. Student, Biomedical Engineering — Pennsylvania State University"
page-layout: article
toc: true
---
```

The rest of the content is identical Markdown.

## The Blog

Quarto's listing feature turns a directory of posts into a browsable index automatically. The `blog/index.qmd` page needs just a few lines:

```yaml
---
title: "Blog"
listing:
  contents: posts
  sort: "date desc"
  type: default
  categories: true
page-layout: full
---
```

Each post lives in its own subdirectory under `blog/posts/` and includes a YAML front matter block with `title`, `date`, `description`, and `categories`. Quarto picks all of this up automatically and builds the listing page, category filters, and RSS feed.

## Automated Deployment with GitHub Actions

The deployment workflow at `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` runs on every push to `main`:

```yaml
name: Deploy to GitHub Pages

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2
      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5
      - uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/render@v2
        with:
          to: html
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: _site

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    permissions:
      pages: write
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
        id: deployment
```

The workflow uses the official `quarto-dev/quarto-actions` to install Quarto and render the project, then hands off the `_site` output directory to GitHub's own deployment actions. No secrets or personal access tokens are required — the `GITHUB_TOKEN` provided automatically by Actions is sufficient.

### One-time Setup in GitHub

After pushing, you need to tell GitHub to use Actions as the Pages source:

1. Go to **Settings → Pages** in your repository.
2. Under **Source**, select **GitHub Actions**.

After that, every push to `main` triggers a new deployment automatically.

## Result

The site now has a clean top navigation bar linking the CV and the blog, a table of contents on longer pages, category filtering on the blog listing, and a GitHub icon linking to my profile. The whole thing is rendered from plain text files and deployed without any manual steps.

Future posts will cover research methods, data analysis workflows, and tools I find useful for biomedical imaging.
